extracted.intended_audience: media critics, journalists, and readers concerned with media accountability
extracted.subtask_description: Opinion/analysis piece evaluating how journalists and media outlets cover allegations of fabrication and how they respond to PR counterattacks; focuses on standards for verification, framing, and accountability. Useful for readers interested in media ethics and news reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read beyond the headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding Bill O’Reilly accountable for his lies would require journalists to read more than just the headline of the charges against him—and that’s never going to happen, says Politico’s Dylan Byers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should absorb the full substance of an exposé rather than relying on headlines or brief summaries. Anti-pattern: treating a story as a simple partisan dispute based on its headline and failing to evaluate the article’s evidence and argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't act as a PR conduit
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a case study in PR: When under attack, be sure to take your counterattack to a media outlet that will pass it along without question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should not uncritically publish or amplify a subject's counterattack. Example: Byers allowed O’Reilly to label Mother Jones's piece a “piece of garbage” and a reporter a “despicable guttersnipe” without investigating the truth of the original charges. Scoring note: linking to or repeating a subject's rebuttal without scrutiny is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify claims with primary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Check primary sources (e.g., video footage) to confirm or refute factual claims — Mother Jones included a video that refuted O’Reilly’s account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an article provides primary evidence that contradicts a public figure’s claim, journalists should view and evaluate that evidence rather than rely on secondhand summaries. Example: the video Mother Jones cited allegedly shows none of the shootings O’Reilly described; journalists should watch such footage before accepting denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false equivalence / ideological 'he said/she said' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not frame well-documented charges of fabrication as an ideological he said/she said, which lets the accused dismiss the charges as partisan attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence weighs clearly on one side, reporting should not reduce the story to symmetrical partisan conflict. Anti-pattern: treating an evidence-backed exposé as merely a partisan dispute because the critics are ideologically opposed to the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent standards across ideological lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect and enforce the same journalistic standards for pundits regardless of ideology; the piece argues conservative pundits often receive lower standards of scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare similar cases (e.g., NBC’s Brian Williams versus Bill O’Reilly) to check for inconsistent accountability. Journalists and editors should explain and justify any differential treatment rather than assume it is normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize semantic defenses that reframe factual claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be skeptical of defenses that rely on semantics (e.g., claiming 'in the Falklands' meant 'in the Falklands War' or was shorthand) when those defenses are used to avoid factual falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between true ambiguity/wording issues and deliberate misrepresentation. Anti-pattern: accepting 'embellishment' explanations that plausibly rewrite the factual record without checking context and likely reader interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check contextual and geographic accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify whether events described actually occurred where and when claimed (e.g., whether British forces attacked mainland Argentina or whether the subject was in the Falklands versus Buenos Aires after the war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy includes geographic and temporal context; mistakes or evasions about where someone was (e.g., claiming to have reported 'in the Falklands') should be tested against historical fact and available records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate critics on substance, not outlet ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dismiss reporting because it comes from a politically identified outlet (e.g., 'they were liberal reporters at an admittedly liberal magazine').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the evidence and reasoning in a critical piece rather than rejecting it on partisan grounds. Anti-pattern: allowing the accused to neutralize a critique by labeling the critic's outlet as ideologically biased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult multiple sources and full reports before judging
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should be expected to read more than one article and to follow the full reporting before forming or repeating judgments about truthfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Byers’ suggestion that reporters need not read two articles is criticized; good practice is to review the full reporting (and related pieces) before accepting or dismissing allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider institutional incentives and accountability mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how news organizations and corporate owners influence disciplinary responses (e.g., Fox/NewsCorp protecting profitable talent versus Comcast/NBC taking different actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of misconduct should include whether institutional economics and PR strategies shape whether and how consequences are applied. Example: profitable personalities may be shielded despite misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place claims and refuting evidence side-by-side in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective exposés present the quoted claim and the documentary evidence that supports or refutes it together (Mother Jones put O’Reilly’s quote next to video that contradicts it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This layout helps readers and other journalists evaluate the dispute; reporters should ensure presentational clarity so that the evidence is evident and assessable, and then follow up rather than ignore it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take embellishments seriously when they alter audience perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat 'major embellishment' as harmless if it changes what audiences would reasonably believe about someone’s experience or credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the practical effect of an embellishment (does it create the impression the subject actually did something they did not?) and pursue correction or accountability when that effect matters; anti-pattern: shrugging that an embellishment 'is not going to lead' to consequences and thus excusing it.
